name: Southern Cook Islands Māori / CIM
confidence_why: The only description of stress, Nicholas's 2016 grammar of Southern Cook Islands Māori, reports from her own recordings that speakers freely alternate between stressing the first mora and the penultimate mora with the conditioning still unresolved, and the other works consulted (Buzacott 1854 and 1878, Buse 1996, Nicholas 2018, Coto-Solano et al. 2022) say nothing about stress.
catalog_citation: Nicholas, Sally Akevai Te Namu. 2016. Ko te Karāma o te Reo Māori o te Pae Tonga o Te Kuki Airani: A Grammar of Southern Cook Islands Māori. PhD thesis, University of Auckland. xxxii+428 pp. hdl:2292/32929 (open access, ResearchSpace).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, 2.9 Stress pp. 51-59; 2.9.1 Word stress p. 52; 2.9.1.3 long vowels p. 55; 2.9.1.6 Summary p. 57; 2.5.2 and 2.9.2 Phrase stress pp. 35, 57-58; 2.4 Phonotactics (syllable weight) p. 33.
catalog_quote: [p. 52, 2.9.1 Word stress:] There are two clear word-stress patterns in evidence. These patterns apply most consistently to words that only contain light syllables but they also apply (less consistently) to words of other forms. In the first pattern, WSP1, the stress falls on the first mora. In the second pattern, WSP2, the stress falls on the penultimate mora (vowel). The use of these patterns varies between speakers. Sometimes an individual speaker will favour one of the patterns. However, a single speaker may also produce both patterns freely. The exact conditions the produce this variation are unclear and require further investigation. [...] [p. 57, 2.9.1.6 Summary:] There are two main word stress patterns that can apply to words of any form. In WSP1 the first mora is stressed and in WSP2 the penultimate mora is stressed. It is not clear what factors influence the choice between WSP1 and WSP2. In words that contain a single long vowel, that syllable may optionally draw the stress, even if that does not conform to WSP1 or WSP2.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (in isolation/citation forms) varies freely between two patterns, both across and within speakers: WSP1 = stress on the first mora, WSP2 = stress on the penultimate mora (the common Polynesian pattern). In CVCV words the two coincide (initial). A single long vowel usually attracts stress (always in trimoraic words), but CVVCVCV words still show either pattern; words with two+ long vowels (>4 morae) show WSP1, penult, or stress on the second long vowel. At phrase level, primary stress is assigned per phonological phrase: penultimate mora of each non-final phrase, with the predicate/focus phrase stressing its lexical head by the word-stress rule and the final phrase doing either; deictic ra/na draw a strong penultimate phrase stress. Author flags the whole account as preliminary ('further research.. required').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Word level: none described. Phrase level (2.5.2, 2.9.2): longer P-phrases may carry one or more secondary stresses; the predicate phrase 'often has a clear secondary stress on the penultimate mora'; author notes the general Polynesian pattern of secondary stress on alternating morae as 'reminiscent' but does not assert it for CIM.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowels optionally attract stress off-pattern; CVCVVCV (loans only) stress the long vowel; words >4 morae with multiple long vowels show a third pattern (stress on second long vowel, e.g. mūˈtēkī); short one-word imperatives; emphatic lengthening stress (2.9.3); pragmatic variation in longer sentences (all lexical heads stressed).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-stress data are elicited citation forms ('words spoken in isolation are the equivalent of a final phrase', Selkirk 1996); author stresses that words are not normally pronounced in isolation and that primary stress is properly a property of the phonological phrase (one main stress per P-phrase, min. 3 morae), usually penultimate mora of the phrase.
new_statements.identity_note: Nicholas (2016) describes Southern Cook Islands Māori as a whole; she states (p. 14 of layout text, ch. 1) that most of her data are in the Rarotongan dialect or the Maꞌuke variety of the Ngā Pū Toru dialect. Stress examples in 2.9 come from Rarotongan/Maꞌuke speakers (Rongo, Maeva, Melota). Glottolog raro1241 'Southern Cook Island Maori' = this language; Rarotongan dialect = raro1242? (dialect-level code not verified here). Note Glottolog's ref 'Bauer 1993 Maori' in the list is a grammar of New Zealand Māori (maor1246), misfiled under raro1241.

sources.note: Ch. 2.9 Stress (pp. 51-59): word stress shows two patterns in free variation across and within speakers - WSP1 stress on first mora, WSP2 stress on penultimate mora; a single long vowel may optionally attract stress; >4-mora words show a third pattern; phrase stress (2.5.2, 2.9.2) is per phonological phrase, usually penultimate mora, predicate head keeps word stress; emphatic lengthening stress (2.9.3). Author calls the account preliminary.
